haiku-low.q1: On-call runs the failover command after 2 of 3 probe locations see 3 consecutive A /healthz failures. Detection only pages on-call; nothing fails over automatically.
haiku-low.q2: It stops, shows the lag, and releases the lock. On-call can rerun with the accept-data-loss override to proceed, or abort.
haiku-low.q3: Promotion needs A fenced and the lag check passed or overridden. B workers need running jobs requeued. DNS needs B scaled and passing health checks.
haiku-low.q4: Sessions are per-region Redis and not replicated, so B holds none from A. Every user must sign in again (accepted).
haiku-low.q5: Its state is snapshotted for review of lost writes, then wiped and rebuilt as B's replica from a base backup of B. No automatic failback.
haiku-low.q6: A's instances self-fence: without a successful control-store read naming A within 15 s, they go read-only. Step 2's privilege revoke is only a backstop.
haiku-low.q7: Control store (3 nodes in A, B, C). Only the failover command, including abort, writes active_region; all instances and workers read it every 5 s.
haiku-low.q8: Step 5 sets jobs marked running in B's database back to queued; B's workers rerun them after step 6. Jobs A finished in its last unreplicated seconds also rerun.
haiku-low.q9: Rerun the command; it resumes at the first unfinished step. Return to A only via abort, before step 4 starts; after that, no return.
haiku-low.q10: Requests reach A until cached DNS expires (60 s max). If A is up, reads are stale and writes get 503; if A is down, requests fail.
haiku-low.q11: Commits B never received (async replication): at most the 30 s lag cap unless overridden. A partitioned A may add up to 20 s more.

sonnet.q1: A failover starts when on-call manually runs the failover command (target B). Detection (2 of 3 probe locations seeing 3 consecutive /healthz failures, probed every 10 s) only pages on-call; nothing fails over automatically.
sonnet.q2: At step 3, if B's recorded lag is over 30 s, the command stops, shows the lag and releases the lock. On-call can then rerun with the accept-data-loss override (proceeds to promotion) or abort (active_region back to A, write privileges restored, log closed). Nothing can write meanwhile.
sonnet.q3: Before promotion (step 4): lock taken, A fenced (active_region = B, privileges revoked best effort, 20 s wait), and lag checked (<=30 s or override). Before B's workers start (step 6): promotion done and jobs marked running by A's workers set back to queued (step 5). Before DNS (step 8): B scaled (step 6) and passes /healthz at its load balancer and from the probes (step 7).
sonnet.q4: Sessions are lost: B's Redis holds no sessions from A (Redis not replicated), so every user must sign in again. This is accepted.
sonnet.q5: A's old database is snapshotted so lost writes can be reviewed, then wiped and rebuilt from a base backup of B as B's replica. No automatic failback; A's app stays read-only; returning to A is a separate planned switchover.
sonnet.q6: The self-fencing rule. Every instance/worker reads active_region from the control store every 5 s and only writes if a successful read within the last 15 s named its own region (write transactions capped at 5 s). A partitioned A either reads B or loses the control store (it cannot get a majority), so it goes read-only (503 on writes, workers stop claiming jobs) within 20 s. The privilege revoke is only a best-effort backstop.
sonnet.q7: The control store (3-node strongly consistent KV cluster, one node each in A, B and C) holds active_region. Only the failover command (including abort) writes it. All app instances and workers in both regions read it every 5 s.
sonnet.q8: At step 5, before any B worker starts, jobs marked running in B's database (all claimed by A's workers) are set back to queued. B's workers rerun them after step 6. Jobs A had finished in its last unreplicated seconds also rerun. Jobs must be idempotent (keyed by job id).
sonnet.q9: Rerun the failover command: it takes the lock (a crashed run's 30 s lease expires within 30 s) and resumes at the first step not logged done; a started but unfinished step is repeated (all steps are safe to repeat). Going back to A is possible only until step 4 is logged as started, via failover --abort (takes lock, sets active_region = A, restores A's write privileges if revoked, closes log). Once step 4 is started, abort is refused even after a crash, and the run only goes forward.
sonnet.q10: From step 2 until its cached DNS expires (up to 60 s after step 8), its requests still go to A. If A is up, its instances are self-fenced: reads work from A's stale database, writes get 503 "read-only, retry shortly". If A is down, requests fail. After the TTL expires, the client reaches B.
sonnet.q11: What is lost is what A committed that B never received (async replication). If A failed outright, no more than B's recorded lag, which step 3 holds to 30 s unless on-call uses the override. If A kept running after B stopped receiving (partition), A's commits up to when it stopped writing (at most 20 s after step 2) are also missing, which step 3 cannot see; they survive only in A's old database snapshot.
